_meta.description: Typological feature explainers: per-feature plain-English names, value code → label maps, MT-relevance notes and citations. Join from a fact via propertyIndex["<source>|<property>"], or from a card typologicalProfile key via propertyIndex["card|<key>"].
_meta.notes: AUTOTYP and other StructureDatasets already store human-readable value labels in the facts DB, so they are rendered as-is and not duplicated here.

wals-1A.name: Consonant Inventories
wals-1A.question: How many distinct consonant sounds the language uses.

2.label: Moderately small
2.plain: Moderately small

wals-1A.mt_relevance: Large or unusual consonant inventories complicate transliteration of names and loanwords.

citation.authors: Ian Maddieson
citation.title: Consonant Inventories (WALS Online chapter 1)

wals-2A.name: Vowel Quality Inventories
wals-2A.question: How many basic vowel qualities the language distinguishes.

2.label: Average (5-6)
2.plain: Average vowel inventory (5-6)

wals-2A.mt_relevance: Vowel-poor or vowel-rich systems reshape borrowed words, affecting named-entity handling.

citation.authors: Ian Maddieson
citation.title: Vowel Quality Inventories (WALS Online chapter 2)

wals-3A.name: Consonant-Vowel Ratio
wals-3A.question: Whether the language has many more consonants than vowels, or a more balanced mix.

2.label: Moderately low
2.plain: Moderately low

wals-3A.mt_relevance: A phonology-level trait that mostly matters for romanization and speech; consonant-heavy words also tend to fragment more under subword tokenizers.

citation.authors: Ian Maddieson
citation.title: Consonant-Vowel Ratio (WALS Online chapter 3)

wals-4A.name: Voicing in Plosives and Fricatives
wals-4A.question: Whether the language distinguishes voiced from voiceless sounds, like 'b' versus 'p'.

2.label: In plosives alone
2.plain: Voicing contrast in plosives alone

4.label: In both plosives and fricatives
4.plain: Voicing contrast in both plosives and fricatives

wals-4A.mt_relevance: Mainly a speech and transliteration issue; when a script under-marks voicing, distinct words can collapse into a single romanized spelling.

citation.authors: Ian Maddieson
citation.title: Voicing in Plosives and Fricatives (WALS Online chapter 4)

wals-5A.property: Voicing and Gaps in Plosive Systems
wals-5A.name: Voicing and Gaps in Plosive Systems
wals-5A.question: Which basic stop consonants (like p, t, k, b, d, g) the language's sound system lacks.

2.label: None missing in /p t k b d g/
2.plain: /p t k b d g/

wals-5A.mt_relevance: Mostly shapes how loanwords are respelled: a missing /p/ or /g/ forces borrowed names into substitute letters, tripping up transliteration.

citation.authors: Ian Maddieson
citation.title: Voicing and Gaps in Plosive Systems (WALS Online chapter 5)

wals-6A.name: Uvular Consonants
wals-6A.question: Whether the language has uvular consonants — 'throaty' sounds far back in the mouth.

2.label: Uvular stops only
2.plain: Uvular stops only

wals-6A.mt_relevance: Chiefly a transliteration concern: uvular sounds map unevenly to Latin letters (q, gh, kh), scattering one name across several spellings.

citation.authors: Ian Maddieson
citation.title: Uvular Consonants (WALS Online chapter 6)

wals-7A.name: Glottalized Consonants
wals-7A.question: Whether the language has glottalized consonants like ejectives or implosives.

2.label: Ejectives only
2.plain: Ejectives only

wals-7A.mt_relevance: These sounds are often written with apostrophes or special marks that noisy text drops, so MT must treat the marked and stripped spellings as one word.

citation.authors: Ian Maddieson
citation.title: Glottalized Consonants (WALS Online chapter 7)

wals-8A.name: Lateral Consonants
wals-8A.question: Which 'l'-like (lateral) consonants the language has, if any.

2.label: /l/, no obstruent laterals
2.plain: /l/, no obstruent laterals

3.label: Laterals, but no /l/, no obstruent laterals
3.plain: Laterals, but no /l/, no obstruent lateral

wals-8A.mt_relevance: Unusual lateral sounds (like Welsh 'll') get romanized as digraphs a tokenizer may split, and their rare letters raise the unknown-token rate.

citation.authors: Ian Maddieson
citation.title: Lateral Consonants (WALS Online chapter 8)

wals-9A.name: The Velar Nasal
wals-9A.question: Whether the language has the 'ng' sound, and whether a word can begin with it.

2.label: No initial velar nasal
2.plain: Velar nasal, but not initially

wals-9A.mt_relevance: Written as a digraph in many scripts, so MT can't always tell a word-initial 'ng' from a separate n-plus-g sequence.

citation.authors: Gregory D.S. Anderson
citation.title: The Velar Nasal (WALS Online chapter 9)

wals-10A.name: Vowel Nasalization
wals-10A.question: Whether the language uses nasal vowels — spoken through the nose — to tell words apart.

2.label: Contrast absent
2.plain: Contrastive nasal vowels absent

wals-10A.mt_relevance: Nasal vowels ride on diacritics like 'ã' that casual text strips, collapsing a nasal word and its oral twin into one spelling.

citation.authors: John Hajek
citation.title: Vowel Nasalization (WALS Online chapter 10)

wals-10B.name: Nasal Vowels in West Africa
wals-10B.question: How many nasal-versus-oral vowel contrasts a language has, and whether nasality spreads.

1.label: no nasal vs. oral vowel contrast
1.plain: no nasal vs. oral vowel contrast

2.label: two-way nasal vs. oral vowel contrast (/ṽ/ vs. /V/) without nasal spreading
2.plain: two-way nasal vs. oral vowel contrast (/ṽ/ vs. /V/) without nasal spreading

3.label: two-way nasal vs. oral vowel contrast (/ṽ/ vs. /V/) with nasal spreading
3.plain: two-way nasal vs. oral vowel contrast (/ṽ/ vs. /V/) with nasal spreading

4.label: four-way nasal vs. oral vowel contrast (/ṽ/ vs. /ṽː/ vs. /V/ vs. /Vː/) without nasal spreading
4.plain: four-way nasal vs. oral vowel contrast (/ṽ/ vs. /ṽː/ vs. /V/ vs. /Vː/) without nasal spreading

5.label: four-way nasal vs. oral vowel contrast (/ṽ/ vs. /ṽː/ vs. /V/ v /Vː/) with nasal spreading
5.plain: four-way nasal vs. oral vowel contrast (/ṽ/ vs. /ṽː/ vs. /V/ v /Vː/) with nasal spreading

wals-10B.mt_relevance: Where nasal contrasts are dense and spread across a word, dropped nasal marks erase several distinctions at once — a recurring West African text issue.

citation.authors: John Hajek
citation.title: Vowel Nasalization (WALS Online chapter 10)

wals-11A.name: Front Rounded Vowels
wals-11A.question: Whether the language has front rounded vowels, like German 'ü' or French 'eu'.

2.label: High and mid
2.plain: High and mid

wals-11A.mt_relevance: These vowels need umlaut letters (ü, ö) that ASCII-only text flattens to u or o, merging words the language keeps distinct.

citation.authors: Ian Maddieson
citation.title: Front Rounded Vowels (WALS Online chapter 11)

wals-12A.name: Syllable Structure
wals-12A.question: How complex a language's syllables can be, from simple ones to heavy consonant clusters.

2.label: Moderately complex
2.plain: Moderately complex syllable structure

wals-12A.mt_relevance: Complex syllables pile up consonant clusters, so subword tokenizers split such words into many short pieces, lengthening sequences and straining alignment.

citation.authors: Ian Maddieson
citation.title: Syllable Structure (WALS Online chapter 12)

wals-13A.name: Tone
wals-13A.question: Whether the language uses pitch (tone) to distinguish word meanings.

2.label: Simple tone system
2.plain: Simple tone system

wals-13A.mt_relevance: Tone is usually invisible in romanized text, so toneless input collapses distinct words into one spelling.

citation.authors: Ian Maddieson
citation.title: Tone (WALS Online chapter 13)

wals-14A.name: Fixed Stress Locations
wals-14A.question: Whether word stress always falls on a fixed syllable, like always the first or last.

2.label: Initial
2.plain: Initial: stress is on the first syllable

3.label: Second
3.plain: Second: stress is on the second syllable

4.label: Third
4.plain: Third: stress is on the third syllable

5.label: Antepenultimate
5.plain: Antepenultimate: stress is on the antepenultimate (third from the right) syllable

6.label: Penultimate
6.plain: Penultimate: stress is on the penultimate (second from the right) syllable

7.label: Ultimate
7.plain: Ultimate: stress is on the ultimate (last) syllable

wals-14A.mt_relevance: Stress is almost never written, so this barely touches text MT; it matters mainly for speech translation and text-to-speech pronunciation.

citation.authors: Rob Goedemans, Harry van der Hulst
citation.title: Fixed Stress Locations (WALS Online chapter 14)

wals-15A.name: Weight-Sensitive Stress
wals-15A.question: Whether stress depends on syllable weight, like vowel length or a closing consonant.

1.label: Left-edge: First or second
1.plain: Left-edge: Stress is on the first or second syllable

2.label: Left-oriented: One of the first three
2.plain: Left-oriented: The third syllable is involved

3.label: Right-edge: Ultimate or penultimate
3.plain: Right-edge: Stress on ultimate or penultimate syllable

4.label: Right-oriented: One of the last three

5.label: Unbounded: Stress can be anywhere
5.plain: Unbounded: Stress can be anywhere in the word

wals-15A.mt_relevance: Syllable-weight stress leaves no mark in ordinary writing, so it bears on speech synthesis and pronunciation rather than translating text.

citation.authors: Rob Goedemans, Harry van der Hulst
citation.title: Weight-Sensitive Stress (WALS Online chapter 15)

wals-16A.property: Weight Factors in Weight-Sensitive Stress Systems
wals-16A.name: Weight Factors in Weight-Sensitive Stress Systems
wals-16A.question: What makes a syllable count as 'heavy' for stress — vowel length or a closing consonant.

1.label: No weight
1.plain: No weight, or weight factor unknown

2.label: Long vowel
2.plain: Long vowel: long vowels are heavy for stress

3.label: Coda consonant
3.plain: Coda consonant: closed syllables are heavy for stress

4.label: Long vowel or coda consonant
4.plain: Long vowel + Coda: long vowels or closed syllables

5.label: Prominence
5.plain: Prominence: other factors are heavy for stress

7.label: Combined
7.plain: Combined: two of the above factors determine weight

wals-16A.mt_relevance: This fine stress detail leaves no trace in spelling, informing pronunciation and speech models rather than text translation.

citation.authors: Rob Goedemans, Harry van der Hulst
citation.title: Weight Factors in Weight-Sensitive Stress Systems (WALS Online chapter 16)

wals-17A.name: Rhythm Types
wals-17A.question: Whether the language's rhythm puts stress at the start (trochaic) or end (iambic) of feet.

1.label: Trochaic
1.plain: Trochaic: left-hand syllable in the foot is strong

2.label: Iambic
2.plain: Iambic: right-hand syllable in the foot is strong

3.label: Dual: both trochaic and iambic
3.plain: Dual: system has both trochaic and iambic feet

wals-17A.mt_relevance: Purely a spoken-rhythm trait — it shapes speech synthesis and prosody, but has almost no effect on written text translation.

citation.authors: Rob Goedemans, Harry van der Hulst
citation.title: Rhythm Types (WALS Online chapter 17)

wals-18A.name: Absence of Common Consonants
wals-18A.question: Whether the language lacks consonants most languages have, like nasals or fricatives.

2.label: No bilabials
2.plain: No bilabials

wals-18A.mt_relevance: A phonological gap: it mostly changes how names and loanwords get spelled and transliterated, with little direct impact on text translation.

citation.authors: Ian Maddieson
citation.title: Absence of Common Consonants (WALS Online chapter 18)

wals-19A.name: Presence of Uncommon Consonants
wals-19A.question: Whether the language has rare consonants like clicks, pharyngeals or 'th' sounds.

2.label: Clicks
2.plain: Clicks

wals-19A.mt_relevance: Rare sounds often need special letters or digraphs, complicating transliteration and name handling more than sentence-level text translation.

citation.authors: Ian Maddieson
citation.title: Presence of Uncommon Consonants (WALS Online chapter 19)

wals-20A.name: Fusion of Selected Inflectional Formatives
wals-20A.question: How tightly the language fuses grammatical markers onto words.

2.label: Exclusively isolating
2.plain: Exclusively isolating

wals-20A.mt_relevance: Highly fused (or highly isolating) word structure changes how much information each token carries for the MT model.

citation.authors: Balthasar Bickel, Johanna Nichols
citation.title: Fusion of Selected Inflectional Formatives (WALS Online chapter 20)

wals-21A.name: Exponence of Selected Inflectional Formatives
wals-21A.question: Whether one case ending marks only case, or fuses it with number, tense or other meanings.

2.label: Case + number
2.plain: Case + number

wals-21A.mt_relevance: Fused endings pack several grammatical meanings into one form, so MT must unpack them to align with languages that mark each separately.

citation.authors: Balthasar Bickel, Johanna Nichols
citation.title: Exponence of Selected Inflectional Formatives (WALS Online chapter 21)

wals-21B.name: Exponence of Tense-Aspect-Mood Inflection
wals-21B.question: Whether a tense-aspect-mood ending also bundles in agreement, voice or polarity.

2.label: TAM+agreement
2.plain: TAM+agreement

wals-21B.mt_relevance: When one tense marker also encodes who acted or whether it's negated, MT must recover meanings the source packs into a single verb ending.

citation.authors: Balthasar Bickel, Johanna Nichols
citation.title: Exponence of Selected Inflectional Formatives (WALS Online chapter 21)

wals-22A.name: Inflectional Synthesis of the Verb
wals-22A.question: How many grammatical categories a single verb form can pack in.

2.label: 2-3 categories per word
2.plain: 2-3 categories per word

wals-22A.mt_relevance: Verbs that encode a whole clause (polysynthesis) explode the vocabulary and defeat word-by-word translation.

citation.authors: Balthasar Bickel, Johanna Nichols
citation.title: Inflectional Synthesis of the Verb (WALS Online chapter 22)

wals-23A.property: Locus of Marking in the Clause
wals-23A.name: Locus of Marking in the Clause
wals-23A.question: Whether clause relations are marked on the verb (head) or on the nouns (dependents).

2.label: Dependent marking
2.plain: P is dependent-marked

wals-23A.mt_relevance: Head- vs dependent-marking changes where affixes attach, so MT must map object marking from a verb to a noun (or vice versa) across the pair.

citation.authors: Johanna Nichols, Balthasar Bickel
citation.title: Locus of Marking in the Clause (WALS Online chapter 23)

wals-24A.property: Locus of Marking in Possessive Noun Phrases
wals-24A.name: Locus of Marking in Possessive Noun Phrases
wals-24A.question: Whether possession is marked on the possessed noun (head) or the possessor (dependent).

2.label: Dependent marking
2.plain: Possessor is dependent-marked

wals-24A.mt_relevance: In some languages the possessed thing takes the mark, in others the owner does — MT must relocate that mark to build a correct possessive.

citation.authors: Johanna Nichols, Balthasar Bickel
citation.title: Locus of Marking in Possessive Noun Phrases (WALS Online chapter 24)

wals-25A.name: Locus of Marking: Whole-language Typology
wals-25A.question: Whether a language marks grammar mostly on heads, on dependents, both, or neither overall.

2.label: Dependent-marking
2.plain: Consistently dependent-marking

wals-25A.mt_relevance: A whole-language summary of where morphology lands — a broad signal of how much affix-shuffling a pair needs, not just one construction.

citation.authors: Johanna Nichols, Balthasar Bickel
citation.title: Locus of Marking: Whole-language Typology (WALS Online chapter 25)

wals-25B.property: Zero Marking of A and P Arguments
wals-25B.name: Zero Marking of A and P Arguments
wals-25B.question: Whether the subject and object of a verb carry no grammatical marking at all.

2.label: Non-zero marking
2.plain: Non-zero marking

wals-25B.mt_relevance: With neither argument marked, word order alone shows who did what, so MT leans on position and can misassign subject and object.

citation.authors: Johanna Nichols, Balthasar Bickel
citation.title: Locus of Marking: Whole-language Typology (WALS Online chapter 25)

wals-26A.property: Prefixing vs. Suffixing in Inflectional Morphology
wals-26A.name: Prefixing vs. Suffixing in Inflectional Morphology
wals-26A.question: Whether grammatical marking mostly attaches before or after the word stem.

2.label: Strongly suffixing
2.plain: Predominantly suffixing

4.label: Equal prefixing and suffixing
4.plain: Approximately equal amounts of suffixing and prefixing

wals-26A.mt_relevance: Prefix- vs suffix-heavy morphology determines where subword tokenizers should split words.

citation.authors: Matthew S. Dryer
citation.title: Prefixing vs. Suffixing in Inflectional Morphology (WALS Online chapter 26)

wals-27A.name: Reduplication
wals-27A.question: Whether the language productively repeats whole or partial words to change meaning.

2.label: Full reduplication only
2.plain: Full reduplication only

wals-27A.mt_relevance: Doubling like 'buku-buku' for plurals maps one word to a phrase, and repeated tokens can trip up MT that treats repetition as an error.

citation.authors: Carl Rubino
citation.title: Reduplication (WALS Online chapter 27)

wals-28A.name: Case Syncretism
wals-28A.question: Whether different cases collapse into one shared form (case syncretism) or stay distinct.

1.label: No case marking
1.plain: Inflectional case marking is absent or minimal

2.label: Core cases only
2.plain: Inflectional case marking is syncretic for core cases only

3.label: Core and non-core
3.plain: Inflectional case marking is syncretic for core and non-core cases

4.label: No syncretism
4.plain: Inflectional case marking is never syncretic

wals-28A.mt_relevance: When one ending covers several cases, the form is ambiguous and MT must use context to tell, say, subject from object apart.

citation.authors: Matthew Baerman, Dunstan Brown
citation.title: Case Syncretism (WALS Online chapter 28)

wals-29A.name: Syncretism in Verbal Person/Number Marking
wals-29A.question: Whether a verb's agreement endings reuse one form across different persons or numbers.

2.label: Syncretic
2.plain: Subject person/number marking is syncretic

3.label: Not syncretic
3.plain: Subject person/number marking is never syncretic

wals-29A.mt_relevance: Shared agreement endings blur which person or number is the subject, so MT may pick the wrong pronoun when translating outward.

citation.authors: Matthew Baerman, Dunstan Brown
citation.title: Syncretism in Verbal Person/Number Marking (WALS Online chapter 29)

wals-30A.name: Number of Genders
wals-30A.question: How many grammatical genders or noun classes the language has.

2.label: Two
2.plain: Two

wals-30A.mt_relevance: Gender systems force MT to choose agreement forms the source language may not specify.

citation.authors: Greville G. Corbett
citation.title: Number of Genders (WALS Online chapter 30)

wals-31A.name: Sex-based and Non-sex-based Gender Systems
wals-31A.question: Whether grammatical gender is assigned by sex, or by other criteria.

2.label: Sex-based
2.plain: Sex-based gender system

wals-31A.mt_relevance: Sex-based gender forces MT to guess the gender of people the source leaves unspecified — a common source of bias errors.

citation.authors: Greville G. Corbett
citation.title: Sex-based and Non-sex-based Gender Systems (WALS Online chapter 31)

wals-32A.name: Systems of Gender Assignment
wals-32A.question: Whether nouns get their gender by meaning, by form, or the language has no gender.

2.label: Semantic
2.plain: Semantic assignment

wals-32A.mt_relevance: How predictably gender is assigned tells MT whether it can infer a noun's gender from meaning or must memorize it word by word.

citation.authors: Greville G. Corbett
citation.title: Systems of Gender Assignment (WALS Online chapter 32)

wals-33A.name: Coding of Nominal Plurality
wals-33A.question: How the language marks that a noun is plural.

2.label: Plural suffix
2.plain: Plural suffix

5.label: Plural complete reduplication
5.plain: Plural by complete reduplication of stem

6.label: Mixed morphological plural
6.plain: Morphological plural with no method primary

wals-33A.mt_relevance: Languages without obligatory plural marking make MT guess number from context.

citation.authors: Matthew S. Dryer
citation.title: Coding of Nominal Plurality (WALS Online chapter 33)

wals-34A.name: Occurrence of Nominal Plurality
wals-34A.question: Whether nouns mark plural, and if so whether it's optional or limited to humans.

2.label: Only human nouns, optional
2.plain: Plural only in human nouns, optional

3.label: Only human nouns, obligatory
3.plain: Plural only in human nouns, obligatory

4.label: All nouns, always optional
4.plain: Plural in all nouns, always optional

5.label: All nouns, optional in inanimates
5.plain: Plural in all nouns, optional in inanimates

6.label: All nouns, always obligatory
6.plain: Plural in all nouns, always obligatory

wals-34A.mt_relevance: When plural is optional or unmarked, MT must guess number from context to render languages like English that force singular vs plural.

citation.authors: Martin Haspelmath
citation.title: Occurrence of Nominal Plurality (WALS Online chapter 34)

wals-35A.name: Plurality in Independent Personal Pronouns
wals-35A.question: Whether plural pronouns like 'we' and 'they' use separate stems or added endings.

2.label: Number-indifferent pronouns
2.plain: Number-indifferent pronouns

5.label: Person-number stem + pronominal plural affix
5.plain: Person-number stem with a pronominal plural affix

6.label: Person-number stem + nominal plural affix
6.plain: Person-number stem with a nominal plural affix

7.label: Person stem + pronominal plural affix
7.plain: Person stem with a pronominal plural affix

8.label: Person stem + nominal plural affix
8.plain: Person stem with a nominal plural affix

wals-35A.mt_relevance: Number-indifferent pronouns leave 'we' vs 'I' unmarked, forcing MT to infer plurality from context to pick the right target pronoun.

citation.authors: Michael Daniel
citation.title: Plurality in Independent Personal Pronouns (WALS Online chapter 35)

wals-36A.name: The Associative Plural
wals-36A.question: Whether the language has an 'and associates' plural, so 'John' can mean 'John's group'.

1.label: Associative same as additive plural
1.plain: Associative plural marker also used for additive plurals

2.label: Unique affixal associative plural
2.plain: Special bound associative plural marker

wals-36A.mt_relevance: Associative plurals ('the Johns' = John's family) have no English word, so MT must unpack them into phrases like 'John and his people'.

citation.authors: Michael Daniel, Edith Moravcsik
citation.title: The Associative Plural (WALS Online chapter 36)

wals-37A.name: Definite Articles
wals-37A.question: Whether the language has a word like "the" for definite nouns.

2.label: Demonstrative word used as definite article
2.plain: Demonstrative word used as marker of definiteness

4.label: No definite, but indefinite article
4.plain: No definite article but indefinite article

wals-37A.mt_relevance: Translating into article languages forces a definiteness choice the source never made.

citation.authors: Matthew S. Dryer
citation.title: Definite Articles (WALS Online chapter 37)

wals-38A.name: Indefinite Articles
wals-38A.question: Whether the language has a word like "a/an" for indefinite nouns.

1.label: Indefinite word distinct from 'one'
1.plain: Indefinite word distinct from numeral for 'one'

2.label: Indefinite word same as 'one'
2.plain: Numeral for 'one' is used as indefinite article

4.label: No indefinite, but definite article
4.plain: No indefinite article but definite article

wals-38A.mt_relevance: Indefinite articles must be inserted or dropped wholesale when translating between article and article-less languages.

citation.authors: Matthew S. Dryer
citation.title: Indefinite Articles (WALS Online chapter 38)

wals-39A.name: Inclusive/Exclusive Distinction in Independent Pronouns
wals-39A.question: Whether 'we' has separate forms for 'we including you' versus 'we but not you'.

2.label: 'We' the same as 'I'
2.plain: 'We' and 'I' identical

wals-39A.mt_relevance: Translating into an inclusive/exclusive 'we' forces a choice English never marks: is the listener part of 'we' or not?

citation.authors: Michael Cysouw
citation.title: Inclusive/Exclusive Distinction in Independent Pronouns (WALS Online chapter 39)

wals-39B.name: Inclusive/Exclusive Forms in Pama-Nyungan
wals-39B.question: Whether this Pama-Nyungan (Australian) language separates inclusive and exclusive 'we'.

2.label: Inclusive and exclusive differentiated
2.plain: Inclusive and exclusive differentiated

wals-39B.mt_relevance: The inclusive/exclusive 'we' split as found in Australian languages: MT into them must decide whether the addressee is inside 'we'.

citation.authors: Michael Cysouw
citation.title: Inclusive/Exclusive Distinction in Independent Pronouns (WALS Online chapter 39)

wals-40A.name: Inclusive/Exclusive Distinction in Verbal Inflection
wals-40A.question: Whether the verb's 'we' agreement distinguishes 'including you' from 'excluding you'.

2.label: 'We' the same as 'I'
2.plain: 'We' and 'I' identical

wals-40A.mt_relevance: Here the inclusive/exclusive choice is baked into verb endings, so MT must resolve who is included even when no pronoun appears.

citation.authors: Michael Cysouw
citation.title: Inclusive/Exclusive Distinction in Verbal Inflection (WALS Online chapter 40)

wals-41A.name: Distance Contrasts in Demonstratives
wals-41A.question: How the language distinguishes "this" and "that" by distance.

2.label: Two-way contrast
2.plain: Two-way contrast

wals-41A.mt_relevance: Demonstrative systems with more (or fewer) distance distinctions than the target force approximation.

citation.authors: Holger Diessel
citation.title: Distance Contrasts in Demonstratives (WALS Online chapter 41)

wals-42A.name: Pronominal and Adnominal Demonstratives
wals-42A.question: Whether 'this' alone ('I want this') differs from 'this' before a noun ('this book').

2.label: Different stem
2.plain: Different stems

wals-42A.mt_relevance: If standalone and noun-modifying demonstratives use different forms, MT must pick the right one based on whether a noun follows.

citation.authors: Holger Diessel
citation.title: Pronominal and Adnominal Demonstratives (WALS Online chapter 42)

wals-43A.name: Third Person Pronouns and Demonstratives
wals-43A.question: Whether third-person pronouns like 'he' or 'they' derive from demonstratives like 'that'.

1.label: Unrelated
1.plain: Third person pronouns and demonstratives are unrelated to demonstratives

2.label: Related for all demonstratives
2.plain: Third person pronouns and demonstratives are related to all demonstratives

3.label: Related to remote demonstratives
3.plain: Third person pronouns and demonstratives are related to remote demonstratives

4.label: Related to non-remote demonstratives
4.plain: Third person pronouns and demonstratives are related to non-remote demonstratives

5.label: Related by gender markers
5.plain: Third person pronouns and demonstratives are related by gender markers

6.label: Related for non-human reference
6.plain: Third person pronouns and demonstratives are related for non-human reference

wals-43A.mt_relevance: Where 'he/she/it' come from 'this/that', pronouns can carry a near/far distance sense that nudges MT's choice of referring word.

citation.authors: D.N.S. Bhat
citation.title: Third Person Pronouns and Demonstratives (WALS Online chapter 43)

wals-44A.property: Gender Distinctions in Independent Personal Pronouns
wals-44A.name: Gender Distinctions in Independent Personal Pronouns
wals-44A.question: Whether pronouns mark gender (he vs she), and in which persons they do so.

1.label: In 3rd person + 1st and/or 2nd person
1.plain: Gender distinctions in 3rd person plus 1st and/or 2nd person

2.label: 3rd person only, but also non-singular
2.plain: Gender distinctions in 3rd person only, but in both singular and non-singular

3.label: 3rd person singular only
3.plain: Gender distinctions in 3rd person singular only

4.label: 1st or 2nd person but not 3rd
4.plain: Gender distinctions in 1st or 2nd person but not 3rd

5.label: 3rd person non-singular only
5.plain: Gender distinctions in 3rd person non-singular only

wals-44A.mt_relevance: Translating into gendered pronouns forces MT to guess he/she/it that a genderless-pronoun source like Turkish never specified.

citation.authors: Anna Siewierska
citation.title: Gender Distinctions in Independent Personal Pronouns (WALS Online chapter 44)

wals-45A.name: Politeness Distinctions in Pronouns
wals-45A.question: Whether pronouns change to show politeness (like French tu/vous).

1.label: No politeness distinction
1.plain: Second person pronouns encode no politeness distinction

2.label: Binary politeness distinction
2.plain: Second person pronouns encode a binary politeness distinction

3.label: Multiple politeness distinctions
3.plain: Second person pronouns encode multiple politeness distinctions

4.label: Pronouns avoided for politeness
4.plain: Second person pronouns are dominantly avoided for politeness reasons

wals-45A.mt_relevance: Politeness distinctions require MT to pick a formality register the source text may not reveal.

citation.authors: Johannes Helmbrecht
citation.title: Politeness Distinctions in Pronouns (WALS Online chapter 45)

wals-46A.name: Indefinite Pronouns
wals-46A.question: How 'someone' and 'something' are formed: from question words, generic nouns, or stems.

2.label: Generic-noun-based
2.plain: Generic-noun-based indefinites

wals-46A.mt_relevance: Interrogative-based indefinites reuse 'who/what' for 'someone/anyone', so MT must tell a question reading from an indefinite one.

citation.authors: Martin Haspelmath
citation.title: Indefinite Pronouns (WALS Online chapter 46)

wals-47A.name: Intensifiers and Reflexive Pronouns
wals-47A.question: Whether emphatic 'himself' (the king himself) matches reflexive 'himself' (cut himself).

1.label: Identical
1.plain: Intensifiers and reflexive pronouns are formally identical

2.label: Differentiated
2.plain: Intensifiers and reflexive pronouns are formally differentiated

wals-47A.mt_relevance: When emphasis and reflexive share one word (English 'himself'), MT must distinguish 'the king himself' from 'cut himself' to translate right.

citation.authors: Ekkehard König, Peter Siemund (Stephan Töpper)
citation.title: Intensifiers and Reflexive Pronouns (WALS Online chapter 47)

wals-48A.name: Person Marking on Adpositions
wals-48A.question: Whether prepositions carry person endings, like a single word for 'to-me' or 'with-us'.

2.label: No person marking
2.plain: Adpositions without person marking

4.label: Pronouns and nouns
4.plain: Person marking for pronouns and nouns

wals-48A.mt_relevance: Person-inflected adpositions fuse 'to me' into one word, so MT must build or split these forms with no separate pronoun to align.

citation.authors: Dik Bakker
citation.title: Person Marking on Adpositions (WALS Online chapter 48)

wals-49A.name: Number of Cases
wals-49A.question: How many grammatical cases nouns can take.

2.label: 2 cases
2.plain: 2 case categories

wals-49A.mt_relevance: Large case systems multiply word forms and demand correct case selection in generation.

citation.authors: Oliver A. Iggesen
citation.title: Number of Cases (WALS Online chapter 49)

wals-50A.name: Asymmetrical Case-Marking
wals-50A.question: Whether case endings mark singular and plural evenly, or one number more than the other.

2.label: Symmetrical
2.plain: Symmetrical case-marking

wals-50A.mt_relevance: Uneven case-marking across number means MT can't reuse one ending pattern; it must track which number gets the extra or missing marker.

citation.authors: Oliver A. Iggesen
citation.title: Asymmetrical Case-Marking (WALS Online chapter 50)

wals-51A.name: Position of Case Affixes
wals-51A.question: Whether case is marked by suffixes, prefixes, or separate words.

2.label: Case prefixes
2.plain: Case prefixes

4.label: Case stem change
4.plain: Case coded by changes within noun stem

5.label: Mixed morphological case
5.plain: Mixed morphological case strategies with none primary

9.label: No case affixes or adpositional clitics
9.plain: Neither case affixes nor adpositional clitics

wals-51A.mt_relevance: Case affixes interact with tokenization: suffix stacking creates rare word forms MT models handle poorly.

citation.authors: Matthew S. Dryer
citation.title: Position of Case Affixes (WALS Online chapter 51)

wals-52A.name: Comitatives and Instrumentals
wals-52A.question: Whether 'with a friend' (company) and 'with a knife' (tool) use the same marker.

2.label: Differentiation
2.plain: Differentiation

wals-52A.mt_relevance: English 'with' covers both company and instrument; MT into a language that splits them must decide which sense each phrase carries.

citation.authors: Thomas Stolz, Cornelia Stroh, Aina Urdze
citation.title: Comitatives and Instrumentals (WALS Online chapter 52)

wals-53A.name: Ordinal Numerals
wals-53A.question: How ordinals like 'first' and 'second' are formed, or if the language has them at all.

1.label: None
1.plain: Zero: Ordinal numerals do not exist

2.label: One, two, three
2.plain: One: No distinction of cardinal and ordinal numerals

3.label: First, two, three
3.plain: First: Cardinal and ordinal numerals are identical except for 'one' and 'first'

4.label: One-th, two-th, three-th
4.plain: One-th: One-th: Ordinal numerals are derived from cardinal numerals

5.label: First/one-th, two-th, three-th
5.plain: First/One-th: All ordinal numerals are derived from cardinal numerals with different allomorphs for 'first' one of which is morphologically independent of 'one'

6.label: First, two-th, three-th
6.plain: Two-th: Two-th: Ordinal numerals from 'two' upwards are derived from cardinal numerals, 'first' is suppletive

7.label: First, second, three-th
7.plain: Second: 'First' and a small set of consecutive higher ordinal numerals are suppletive

wals-53A.mt_relevance: Irregular 'first/second' beside regular 'third, fourth' means MT can't just add an ending; suppletive ordinals must be learned per language.

citation.authors: Thomas Stolz, Ljuba N. Veselinova
citation.title: Ordinal Numerals (WALS Online chapter 53)

wals-54A.name: Distributive Numerals
wals-54A.question: Whether the language marks distributive numerals like 'one each' or 'two apiece'.

2.label: Marked by reduplication
2.plain: Marked by reduplication

7.label: Marked by mixed or other strategies
7.plain: Marked by mixed or other strategies

wals-54A.mt_relevance: A distributive form like 'two apiece' rarely has a one-word match, so MT must unpack it into a phrase or drop the 'each' entirely.

citation.authors: David Gil
citation.title: Distributive Numerals (WALS Online chapter 54)

wals-55A.name: Numeral Classifiers
wals-55A.question: Whether counting requires a classifier word (like "three head of cattle" for everything).

2.label: Optional
2.plain: Numeral classifiers are optional

wals-55A.mt_relevance: Classifier languages need the right classifier per noun, which MT must select without an equivalent cue in the source.

citation.authors: David Gil
citation.title: Numeral Classifiers (WALS Online chapter 55)

wals-56A.name: Conjunctions and Universal Quantifiers
wals-56A.question: Whether the word for 'and' looks like the word for 'all' or 'every'.

2.label: Formally similar, without interrogative
2.plain: Formally similar, not involving interrogative expression

wals-56A.mt_relevance: When 'and' and 'every' share a form, a system can misread coordination as quantification, confusing which nouns are listed versus totalled.

citation.authors: David Gil
citation.title: Conjunctions and Universal Quantifiers (WALS Online chapter 56)

wals-57A.name: Position of Pronominal Possessive Affixes
wals-57A.question: Whether possessive marking sits on the owner or the thing owned.

2.label: Possessive suffixes
2.plain: Possessive suffixes

3.label: Prefixes and suffixes
3.plain: Both possessive prefixes and possessive suffixes, with neither primary

wals-57A.mt_relevance: Possession marked on the possessed noun (head-marking) reverses the structure MT expects from European languages.

citation.authors: Matthew S. Dryer
citation.title: Position of Pronominal Possessive Affixes (WALS Online chapter 57)

wals-58A.name: Obligatory Possessive Inflection
wals-58A.question: Whether some nouns (like body parts or kin) must always be marked as possessed.

2.label: Absent
2.plain: No obligatorily possessed nouns

wals-58A.mt_relevance: Into such a language, MT must invent a possessor — bare 'hand' has to become 'someone's hand', since unpossessed forms are ungrammatical.

citation.authors: Balthasar Bickel, Johanna Nichols
citation.title: Obligatory Possessive Inflection (WALS Online chapter 58)

wals-58B.name: Number of Possessive Nouns
wals-58B.question: How many nouns the language requires to always appear possessed (none, one, a few, many).

2.label: One
2.plain: One

wals-58B.mt_relevance: The more such nouns, the more often MT into the language must supply a possessor the source left implicit.

citation.authors: Balthasar Bickel, Johanna Nichols
citation.title: Obligatory Possessive Inflection (WALS Online chapter 58)

wals-59A.name: Possessive Classification
wals-59A.question: Whether the language sorts nouns into possession classes like alienable vs. inalienable.

2.label: Two classes
2.plain: Two classes

wals-59A.mt_relevance: Each class uses a different 'my/your' construction, so MT must know a noun's class before it can build the possessive phrase.

citation.authors: Johanna Nichols, Balthasar Bickel
citation.title: Possessive Classification (WALS Online chapter 59)

wals-60A.name: Genitives, Adjectives and Relative Clauses
wals-60A.question: Whether possessors, adjectives and relative clauses are marked alike or kept distinct.

2.label: Genitives and adjectives collapsed
2.plain: Moderately differentiated, with genitives and adjectives collapsed

3.label: Genitives and relative clauses collapsed
3.plain: Moderately differentiated, with genitives and relative clauses collapsed

4.label: Adjectives and relative clauses collapsed
4.plain: Moderately differentiated, with adjectives and relative clauses collapsed

wals-60A.mt_relevance: When one marker covers possession, adjectives and relatives alike, MT must guess which modifier relation is meant before reordering it.

citation.authors: David Gil
citation.title: Genitives, Adjectives and Relative Clauses (WALS Online chapter 60)

wals-61A.name: Adjectives without Nouns
wals-61A.question: Whether an adjective can stand alone without a noun, as in 'the poor'.

1.label: Not without noun
1.plain: Adjective may not occur without noun

2.label: Without marking
2.plain: Adjective may occur without noun, and without marking

3.label: Marked by prefix
3.plain: Adjective may occur without noun, obligatorily marked by prefix

4.label: Marked by suffix
4.plain: Adjective may occur without noun, obligatorily marked by suffix

5.label: Marked by preceding word
5.plain: Adjective may occur without noun, obligatorily marked by preceding word

6.label: Marked by following word
6.plain: Adjective may occur without noun, obligatorily marked by following word

7.label: Marked by mixed or other strategies
7.plain: Adjective may occur without noun, obligatorily marked by mixed or other strategies

wals-61A.mt_relevance: Into languages that require extra marking here, MT must nominalize a bare adjective — turning 'poor' into a proper 'the poor one' form.

citation.authors: David Gil
citation.title: Adjectives without Nouns (WALS Online chapter 61)

wals-62A.name: Action Nominal Constructions
wals-62A.question: How the language turns a clause into a noun phrase, like 'the destruction of the city'.

1.label: Sentential
1.plain: Sentential: dependent-marking of the finite clause is retained for S, A and P

2.label: Possessive-Accusative
2.plain: Possessive-Accusative: S/A treated as possessors, P retains sentential marking

3.label: Ergative-Possessive
3.plain: Ergative-Possessive: S/P treated as possessors, A treated differently

4.label: Double-Possessive
4.plain: Double-Possessive: All major arguments treated as possessors

6.label: Mixed
6.plain: Mixed: Several patterns in the same language

7.label: Restricted
7.plain: Not both A and P in the same construction

wals-62A.mt_relevance: Nominalizations often recode subject and object as possessors, so MT must recover who acted on whom before rendering it in the target.

citation.authors: Maria Koptjevskaja-Tamm
citation.title: Action Nominal Constructions (WALS Online chapter 62)

wals-63A.name: Noun Phrase Conjunction
wals-63A.question: Whether the language uses the same word for 'and' and 'with'.

2.label: 'And' identical to 'with'
2.plain: WITH-languages: 'and' and 'with' are identical

wals-63A.mt_relevance: In 'with'-languages 'John and Mary' looks like 'John with Mary', so MT must decide whether it is coordination or an accompaniment phrase.

citation.authors: Leon Stassen
citation.title: Noun Phrase Conjunction (WALS Online chapter 63)

wals-64A.name: Nominal and Verbal Conjunction
wals-64A.question: Whether joining two nouns uses the same 'and' as joining two verbs or clauses.

1.label: Identity
1.plain: Nominal and verbal conjunction are largely identical

2.label: Differentiation
2.plain: Nominal and verbal conjunction are different

3.label: Both expressed by juxtaposition
3.plain: Nominal and verbal conjunction are primarily expressed by juxtaposition

wals-64A.mt_relevance: If nouns and verbs take different connectives, MT must pick the right 'and' based on what it is joining, not reuse one word.

citation.authors: Martin Haspelmath
citation.title: Nominal and Verbal Conjunction (WALS Online chapter 64)

wals-65A.name: Perfective/Imperfective Aspect
wals-65A.question: Whether verbs grammatically mark perfective vs imperfective aspect.

2.label: No grammatical marking
2.plain: No grammatical marking of perfective/imperfective distinction

wals-65A.mt_relevance: Aspect choices (e.g. Slavic verb pairs) must be inferred when the source language does not mark them.

citation.authors: Östen Dahl, Viveka Velupillai
citation.title: Perfective/Imperfective Aspect (WALS Online chapter 65)

wals-66A.name: The Past Tense
wals-66A.question: Whether the language marks past tense on verbs, and how many degrees of remoteness.

1.label: Present, no remoteness distinctions
1.plain: Past/non-past distinction marked; no remoteness distinction

2.label: Present, 2-3 remoteness distinctions
2.plain: Past/non-past distinction marked; 2-3 degrees of remoteness distinguished

3.label: Present, 4 or more remoteness distinctions
3.plain: Past/non-past distinction marked; at least 4 degrees of remoteness distinguished

4.label: No past tense
4.plain: No grammatical marking of past/non-past distinction

wals-66A.mt_relevance: Languages with remoteness distinctions (recent vs distant past) need temporal context the source rarely gives.

citation.authors: Östen Dahl, Viveka Velupillai
citation.title: The Past Tense (WALS Online chapter 66)

wals-67A.name: The Future Tense
wals-67A.question: Whether the language marks future time grammatically.

2.label: No inflectional future
2.plain: No inflectional marking of future/non-future distinction

wals-67A.mt_relevance: Inflectional futures must be chosen or dropped when the source expresses futurity lexically.

citation.authors: Östen Dahl, Viveka Velupillai
citation.title: The Future Tense (WALS Online chapter 67)

wals-68A.name: The Perfect
wals-68A.question: Whether the language has a perfect form like 'has eaten', and where that form came from.

1.label: From possessive
1.plain: Perfect of the 'have'-type (derived from a possessive construction)

2.label: From 'finish', 'already'
2.plain: Perfect derived from word meaning 'finish' or 'already'

wals-68A.mt_relevance: The perfect-vs-past line falls in different places across languages, so MT often picks the wrong one — 'I ate' vs 'I have eaten'.

citation.authors: Östen Dahl, Viveka Velupillai
citation.title: The Perfect (WALS Online chapter 68)

wals-69A.name: Position of Tense-Aspect Affixes
wals-69A.question: Where tense and aspect markers sit relative to the verb stem.

2.label: Tense-aspect suffixes
2.plain: Tense-aspect suffixes

4.label: Mixed type
4.plain: Combination of tense-aspect strategies with none primary

wals-69A.mt_relevance: Affix position shapes subword segmentation and the locality of grammatical cues.

citation.authors: Matthew S. Dryer
citation.title: Position of Tense-Aspect Affixes (WALS Online chapter 69)

wals-70A.name: The Morphological Imperative
wals-70A.question: How the language forms commands (imperatives).

1.label: Second singular and second plural
1.plain: The language has morphologically dedicated second singular as well as second plural imperatives

2.label: Second singular
2.plain: The language has morphologically dedicated second singular imperatives but no morphologically dedicated second plural imperatives

3.label: Second plural
3.plain: The language has morphologically dedicated second plural imperatives but no morphologically dedicated second singular imperatives

4.label: Second person number-neutral
4.plain: The language has morphologically dedicated second person imperatives that do not distinguish between singular and plural

5.label: No second-person imperatives
5.plain: The language has no morphologically dedicated second-person imperatives at all

wals-70A.mt_relevance: Dedicated imperative morphology must be selected correctly for instructions and UI text.

citation.authors: Johan van der Auwera, Ludo Lejeune (Umarani Pappuswamy, Valentin Goussev)
citation.title: The Morphological Imperative (WALS Online chapter 70)

wals-71A.name: The Prohibitive
wals-71A.question: How the language forms a negative command like 'don't go!'.

1.label: Normal imperative + normal negative
1.plain: The prohibitive uses the verbal construction of the second singular imperative and a sentential negative strategy found in (indicative) declaratives

2.label: Normal imperative + special negative
2.plain: The prohbitive uses the verbal construction of the second singular imperative and a sentential negative strategy not found in (indicative) declaratives

3.label: Special imperative + normal negative
3.plain: The prohibitive uses a verbal construction other than the second singular imperative and a sentential negative strategy found in (indicative) declaratives

4.label: Special imperative + special negative
4.plain: The prohibitive uses a verbal construction other than the second singular imperative and a sentential negative strategy not found in (indicative) declaratives

wals-71A.mt_relevance: A prohibitive may need a special verb form or negator, not just the imperative plus 'not', so MT must build the exact forbidding shape.

citation.authors: Johan van der Auwera, Ludo Lejeune (Valentin Goussev)
citation.title: The Prohibitive (WALS Online chapter 71)

wals-72A.name: Imperative-Hortative Systems
wals-72A.question: How many persons the language can give commands to, from 'go!' to 'let's go'.

1.label: Maximal system
1.plain: The language has a maximal system, but not a minimal one

2.label: Minimal system
2.plain: The language has a minimal system, but not a maximal one

3.label: Both types of system
3.plain: The language has both a maximal and a minimal system

4.label: Neither type of system
4.plain: The language has neither a maximal nor a minimal system

wals-72A.mt_relevance: Systems differ in which persons take a command form, so MT must map English 'let's'/'let him' phrases onto (or out of) dedicated hortative inflections.

citation.authors: Johan van der Auwera, Nina Dobrushina, Valentin Goussev
citation.title: Imperative-Hortative Systems (WALS Online chapter 72)

wals-73A.name: The Optative
wals-73A.question: Whether the language has a special verb form for wishes, like 'may you live long'.

2.label: Inflectional optative absent
2.plain: Inflectional optative absent

wals-73A.mt_relevance: A dedicated wish form has no single English match, so MT must render it with 'may...' or 'if only...' — and detect those when going the other way.

citation.authors: Nina Dobrushina, Johan van der Auwera, Valentin Goussev
citation.title: The Optative (WALS Online chapter 73)

wals-74A.name: Situational Possibility
wals-74A.question: How the language expresses situational possibility — being able to do something.

1.label: Affixes on verbs
1.plain: The language can express situational possibility with affixes on verbs

2.label: Verbal constructions
2.plain: The language cannot express situational possibility with affixes on verbs, but with verbal constructions

3.label: Other kinds of markers
3.plain: The language cannot express situational possibility with affixes on verbs or with verbal constructions, but with other kinds of markers

wals-74A.mt_relevance: Whether ability is an affix or a separate word changes how many tokens carry 'can', complicating alignment and modal choice.

citation.authors: Johan van der Auwera, Andreas Ammann
citation.title: Situational Possibility (WALS Online chapter 74)

wals-75A.name: Epistemic Possibility
wals-75A.question: How the language marks epistemic possibility — that something may or might be true.

1.label: Verbal constructions
1.plain: The language can express epistemic possibility with verbal constructions

2.label: Affixes on verbs
2.plain: The language cannot express epistemic possibility with verbal constructions, but with affixes on verbs

3.label: Other
3.plain: The language cannot express epistemic possibility with verbal constructions or with affixes on verbs, but with other kinds of markers

wals-75A.mt_relevance: Epistemic 'might/may' can be an affix or an auxiliary, and the target may force a certainty level the source left unstated.

citation.authors: Johan van der Auwera, Andreas Ammann
citation.title: Epistemic Possibility (WALS Online chapter 75)

wals-76A.property: Overlap between Situational and Epistemic Modal Marking
wals-76A.name: Overlap between Situational and Epistemic Modal Marking
wals-76A.question: Whether a single marker covers both ability (situational) and likelihood (epistemic).

1.label: Overlap for both possibility and necessity
1.plain: The language has markers that can code both situational and epistemic modality, both for possibility and necessity

2.label: Overlap for either possibility or necessity
2.plain: The language has markers that can code both situational and epistemic modality, but only for possibility or for necessity

3.label: No overlap
3.plain: The language has no markers that can code both situational and epistemic modality

wals-76A.mt_relevance: One marker for both readings is ambiguous — MT must decide if it means 'is able to' or 'is likely to' and can pick the wrong one.

citation.authors: Johan van der Auwera, Andreas Ammann
citation.title: Overlap between Situational and Epistemic Modal Marking (WALS Online chapter 76)

wals-77A.name: Semantic Distinctions of Evidentiality
wals-77A.question: Whether speakers must grammatically mark how they know what they say (evidentiality).

2.label: Indirect only
2.plain: Only indirect evidentials

wals-77A.mt_relevance: Evidential systems force MT to state an information source (seen, heard, inferred) that the source text never specifies.

citation.authors: Ferdinand de Haan
citation.title: Semantic Distinctions of Evidentiality (WALS Online chapter 77)

wals-78A.name: Coding of Evidentiality
wals-78A.question: How evidentiality is expressed — by affixes, particles, or tense forms.

2.label: Verbal affix or clitic
2.plain: Verbal affix or clitic

wals-78A.mt_relevance: Evidential affixes are obligatory in some languages; omitting them produces ungrammatical or misleading output.

citation.authors: Ferdinand de Haan
citation.title: Coding of Evidentiality (WALS Online chapter 78)

wals-79A.property: Suppletion According to Tense and Aspect
wals-79A.name: Suppletion According to Tense and Aspect
wals-79A.question: Whether verbs switch to a whole different stem across tenses or aspects (like go/went).

2.label: Aspect
2.plain: Suppletion according to aspect

3.label: Tense and aspect
3.plain: Suppletion in both tense and aspect

4.label: None
4.plain: No suppletion in tense or aspect

wals-79A.mt_relevance: Suppletive stems like go→went share no letters, so a system must memorize them as whole forms rather than derive them by rule.

citation.authors: Ljuba N. Veselinova
citation.title: Suppletion According to Tense and Aspect (WALS Online chapter 79)

wals-79B.name: Suppletion in Imperatives and Hortatives
wals-79B.question: Whether commands and 'let's' (hortative) forms use a completely different verb stem.

1.label: A regular and a suppletive form alternate
1.plain: A regular and a suppletive form alternate

2.label: Imperative
2.plain: Imperative

5.label: None (= no suppletive imperatives reported in the reference material)
5.plain: None (= no suppletive imperatives reported in the reference material)

wals-79B.mt_relevance: Irregular command and 'let's' stems can't be built from the base verb, so MT must learn each suppletive imperative on its own.

citation.authors: Ljuba N. Veselinova
citation.title: Suppletion According to Tense and Aspect (WALS Online chapter 79)

wals-80A.name: Verbal Number and Suppletion
wals-80A.question: Whether the verb changes form for how many participants or events (verbal number).

2.label: Singular-plural pairs, no suppletion
2.plain: Singular-plural pairs, no suppletion

wals-80A.mt_relevance: Some languages pick a different verb for one vs many participants — a distinction most source languages mark on the noun, not the verb.

citation.authors: Ljuba N. Veselinova
citation.title: Verbal Number and Suppletion (WALS Online chapter 80)

wals-81A.property: Order of Subject, Object and Verb
wals-81A.name: Order of Subject, Object and Verb
wals-81A.question: The dominant order of subject, object and verb in a plain sentence.

2.label: SVO
2.plain: Subject-verb-object (SVO)

wals-81A.mt_relevance: Basic word order is the single biggest driver of reordering between language pairs (e.g. SOV ↔ SVO).

citation.authors: Matthew S. Dryer
citation.title: Order of Subject, Object and Verb (WALS Online chapter 81)

wals-81B.property: Languages with two Dominant Orders of Subject, Object, and Verb
wals-81B.name: Languages with two Dominant Orders of Subject, Object, and Verb
wals-81B.question: Which two basic subject-object-verb orders the language uses about equally.

2.label: VSO or VOS
2.plain: VSO or VOS

wals-81B.mt_relevance: With two competing basic orders, reordering into the target isn't fixed — MT must choose per sentence, raising the odds of a scrambled clause.

citation.authors: Matthew S. Dryer
citation.title: Order of Subject, Object and Verb (WALS Online chapter 81)

wals-82A.name: Order of Subject and Verb

2.plain: Double-headed or RelN

wals-91A.property: Order of Degree Word and Adjective

3.label: Mixed

wals-94A.property: Order of Adverbial Subordinator and Clause

wals-95A.property: Relationship between the Order of Object and Verb and the Order of Adposition and Noun Phrase

2.plain: Object-verb and noun-relative clause (OV&NRel)

5.label: Other

wals-97A.property: Relationship between the Order of Object and Verb and the Order of Adjective and Noun

wals-97A.question: How verb–object order relates to other word-order traits in this language.

2.label: OV and NAdj
2.plain: Object-verb and noun-adjective (OV&NAdj)

5.label: Other

wals-98A.property: Alignment of Case Marking of Full Noun Phrases

2.label: Nominative - accusative (standard)
2.plain: Nominative - accusative (standard)

2.label: Nominative - accusative (standard)
2.plain: Nominative - accusative (standard)

6.plain: Zero realization only of third person non-singular

wals-104A.property: Order of Person Markers on the Verb

2.label: Absent

4.plain: Negative word, unclear if verb or particle

5.plain: Variation between negative word and affix

2.label: Nonverbal encoding

wals-118A.mt_relevance: Verb-like adjectives carry tense and need no 'to be', so MT must insert or delete a copula when translating them.

citation.authors: Leon Stassen
citation.title: Predicative Adjectives (WALS Online chapter 118)

wals-119A.name: Nominal and Locational Predication
wals-119A.question: Whether 'she is a teacher' and 'she is at home' use the same linking construction.

1.label: Different
1.plain: Split (i.e. different) encoding of nominal and locational predication

2.label: Identical
2.plain: Shared (i.e. identical) encoding of nominal and locational predication

wals-119A.mt_relevance: Some languages use different copulas for identity vs location, like Spanish ser/estar, so MT must pick the correct one.

citation.authors: Leon Stassen
citation.title: Nominal and Locational Predication (WALS Online chapter 119)

wals-120A.name: Zero Copula for Predicate Nominals
wals-120A.question: Whether the language can drop the linking verb in 'she (is) a doctor'.

2.label: Possible
2.plain: Zero copula is possible

wals-120A.mt_relevance: From a copula-dropping language MT must supply 'is/are'; into one it should delete the copula to sound natural.

citation.authors: Leon Stassen
citation.title: Zero Copula for Predicate Nominals (WALS Online chapter 120)

wals-121A.name: Comparative Constructions
wals-121A.question: How the language says one thing exceeds another, as in 'taller than X'.

2.label: Exceed
2.plain: Exceed Comparative

wals-121A.mt_relevance: 'Than' has no counterpart in exceed-type ('tall surpasses X') or conjoined ('this tall, that short') comparisons, so MT must recast them.

citation.authors: Leon Stassen
citation.title: Comparative Constructions (WALS Online chapter 121)

wals-122A.name: Relativization on Subjects
wals-122A.question: How the language builds relative clauses like 'the man who left', on the subject.

2.label: Non-reduction
2.plain: Non-reduction

wals-122A.mt_relevance: Some languages leave a gap in the subject slot while others keep a resumptive pronoun ('the man that he left'), so MT must insert or delete it.

citation.authors: Bernard Comrie, Tania Kuteva
citation.title: Relativization on Subjects (WALS Online chapter 122)

wals-123A.name: Relativization on Obliques
wals-123A.question: How the language forms relative clauses on oblique roles (e.g. 'the man I gave it to').

2.label: Non-reduction
2.plain: Non-Reduction Strategy

wals-123A.mt_relevance: Relativizing an oblique like 'the house I live in' may need a resumptive pronoun in one language but a gap in another — MT must insert or delete it.

citation.authors: Bernard Comrie, Tania Kuteva
citation.title: Relativization on Obliques (WALS Online chapter 123)

wals-124A.name: 'Want' Complement Subjects
wals-124A.question: Whether 'want' phrases leave the subject implicit ('want to go') or state it overtly.

1.label: Subject is left implicit
1.plain: The complement subject is left implicit

2.label: Subject is expressed overtly
2.plain: The complement subject is expressed overtly

4.label: Desiderative verbal affix
4.plain: 'Want' is expressed as a desiderative verbal affix

5.label: Desiderative particle
5.plain: 'Want' is expressed as an uninflected desiderative particle

wals-124A.mt_relevance: Translating into a language that restates the subject, MT must supply a pronoun the source's 'want to go' construction left unspoken.

citation.authors: Martin Haspelmath
citation.title: 'Want' Complement Subjects (WALS Online chapter 124)

wals-125A.name: Purpose Clauses
wals-125A.question: Whether purpose clauses ('in order to…') use a full finite verb or a reduced verb form.

2.label: Balanced/deranked
2.plain: Balanced/deranked

wals-125A.mt_relevance: Deranked purpose verbs (infinitives or special forms) must be expanded into or collapsed from full 'so that' clauses across languages.

citation.authors: Sonia Cristofaro
citation.title: Purpose Clauses (WALS Online chapter 125)

wals-126A.name: 'When' Clauses
wals-126A.question: Whether 'when' time clauses use a full finite verb or a reduced (non-finite) verb form.

2.label: Balanced/deranked
2.plain: Balanced/deranked

wals-126A.mt_relevance: A deranked 'when' verb often drops tense and subject marking, which MT must reconstruct when the target language wants a full clause.

citation.authors: Sonia Cristofaro
citation.title: 'When' Clauses (WALS Online chapter 126)

wals-127A.name: Reason Clauses
wals-127A.question: Whether reason clauses ('because…') use a full finite verb or a reduced verb form.

2.label: Balanced/deranked
2.plain: Balanced/deranked

wals-127A.mt_relevance: Reduced reason clauses can blur cause and purpose, so MT risks translating 'because' as 'in order to' or vice versa.

citation.authors: Sonia Cristofaro
citation.title: Reason Clauses (WALS Online chapter 127)

wals-128A.name: Utterance Complement Clauses
wals-128A.question: Whether 'say/tell' complement clauses use a full finite verb or a reduced verb form.

2.label: Balanced/deranked
2.plain: Balanced/deranked

wals-128A.mt_relevance: Reported speech shifts: a finite 'that…' complement needs a complementizer plus tense and pronoun changes a deranked source verb doesn't carry.

citation.authors: Sonia Cristofaro
citation.title: Utterance Complement Clauses (WALS Online chapter 128)

wals-129A.name: Hand and Arm
wals-129A.question: Whether "hand" and "arm" are the same word or different words.

2.label: Different
2.plain: Differentiation: one word denotes 'hand' and another, different word denotes 'arm'

wals-129A.mt_relevance: A classic lexical-split example: one source word maps to two target words and MT must pick by context.

citation.authors: Cecil H. Brown
citation.title: Hand and Arm (WALS Online chapter 129)

wals-130A.name: Finger and Hand
wals-130A.question: Whether one word means both 'hand' and 'finger' or the two have separate words.

1.label: Identical
1.plain: Identity: a single word denotes both 'hand' and 'finger' and/or 'fingers'

2.label: Different
2.plain: Differentiation: one word denotes 'hand' and another, different word denotes 'finger' (or, very rarely, 'fingers')

wals-130A.mt_relevance: A single word for both 'hand' and 'finger' forces MT to pick the right one from context; mostly a word-choice, not structural, issue.

citation.authors: Cecil H. Brown
citation.title: Finger and Hand (WALS Online chapter 130)

wals-130B.property: Cultural Categories of Languages with Identity of 'Finger' and 'Hand'

wals-130B.question: Whether speakers who merge 'hand' and 'finger' are foragers, mixed, or full farmers.

2.label: Farmer-foragers
2.plain: Farmer-foragers

wals-130B.mt_relevance: This is ethnographic metadata about subsistence economy, not a grammatical trait — effectively no impact on text translation.

citation.authors: Cecil H. Brown
citation.title: Finger and Hand (WALS Online chapter 130)

wals-131A.name: Numeral Bases

2.label: Hybrid vigesimal-decimal
2.plain: Hybrid vigesimal-decimal

wals-131A.mt_relevance: Non-decimal or restricted number systems may lack words for large or exact numbers, forcing MT to paraphrase or fall back on digits.

citation.authors: Bernard Comrie
citation.title: Numeral Bases (WALS Online chapter 131)

wals-132A.property: Number of Non-Derived Basic Colour Categories

wals-132A.question: How many basic, non-derived colour words the language has, from 3 up to 5.5.

2.plain: Between 3 and 4 categories

wals-132A.mt_relevance: With only a few basic colour words, one term spans several hues, so MT must guess the exact shade a target language names on its own.

citation.authors: Paul Kay, Luisa Maffi
citation.title: Number of Non-Derived Basic Colour Categories (WALS Online chapter 132)

wals-133A.name: Number of Basic Colour Categories
wals-133A.question: How many basic colour categories the language names in total, from 3-4 up to 9-10.

2.plain: Between 4 and 5, 5, or between 5 and 6 categories

wals-133A.mt_relevance: Colour vocabularies split unevenly, so a hue named in the source may have no single word in the target, forcing a descriptive paraphrase.

citation.authors: Paul Kay, Luisa Maffi
citation.title: Number of Basic Colour Categories (WALS Online chapter 133)

wals-134A.name: Green and Blue
wals-134A.question: Whether the language separates 'green' and 'blue' or merges them into one 'grue' term.

2.label: Green/blue
2.plain: Green-or-blue ('grue')

7.label: None
7.plain: Green and blue not both encoded in any basic color term

wals-134A.mt_relevance: A single 'grue' word can't be cleanly split into 'green' or 'blue' when translating out, so MT must guess which the writer meant.

citation.authors: Paul Kay, Luisa Maffi
citation.title: Green and Blue (WALS Online chapter 134)

wals-135A.name: Red and Yellow
wals-135A.question: Whether the language separates 'red' and 'yellow' or covers both with one word.

2.label: Red/yellow
2.plain: Red-or-yellow

5.label: None
5.plain: Red and yellow not both encoded in any basic color term

wals-135A.mt_relevance: When one term covers both red and yellow, MT into a colour-splitting language must choose one and can pick the wrong shade.

citation.authors: Paul Kay, Luisa Maffi
citation.title: Red and Yellow (WALS Online chapter 135)

wals-136A.name: M-T Pronouns
wals-136A.question: Whether the language has distinct words for "m" and "n" sounds — an areal lexical trait (M-T pronouns).

2.label: M-T pronouns, paradigmatic
2.plain: M-T pronouns, paradigmatic

wals-136A.mt_relevance: Mostly of historical interest; little direct effect on machine translation.

citation.authors: Johanna Nichols, David A. Peterson
citation.title: M-T Pronouns (WALS Online chapter 136)

wals-136B.name: M in First Person Singular
wals-136B.question: Whether the word for 'I/me' contains an 'm' sound, as in English 'me' and 'my'.

1.label: No m in first person singular
1.plain: No m in first person singular

2.label: m in first person singular
2.plain: m in first person singular

wals-136B.mt_relevance: This is a historical sound pattern in the pronoun, not a grammar rule — essentially no effect on text translation quality.

citation.authors: Johanna Nichols, David A. Peterson
citation.title: M-T Pronouns (WALS Online chapter 136)

wals-137A.name: N-M Pronouns
wals-137A.question: Whether first-person pronouns use an 'n' sound and second-person an 'm' sound.

2.label: N-M pronouns, paradigmatic
2.plain: N-M pronouns, paradigmatic

wals-137A.mt_relevance: A historical sound pattern in pronoun forms; essentially no effect on how a text-translation system handles pronouns as whole words.

citation.authors: Johanna Nichols, David A. Peterson
citation.title: N-M Pronouns (WALS Online chapter 137)

wals-137B.name: M in Second Person Singular
wals-137B.question: Whether the word for singular 'you' contains an 'm' sound.

1.label: No m in second person singular
1.plain: No m in second person singular

2.label: m in second person singular
2.plain: m in second person singular

wals-137B.mt_relevance: A lexical sound trait of a single pronoun; negligible impact on text translation, which treats each pronoun as one token.

citation.authors: Johanna Nichols, David A. Peterson
citation.title: N-M Pronouns (WALS Online chapter 137)

wals-138A.name: Tea
wals-138A.question: What the word for "tea" reveals about trade routes (te vs cha).

2.label: Words derived from Min Nan Chinese te
2.plain: Words derived from Min Nan Chinese te

wals-138A.mt_relevance: Loanword pathways predict how the language adapts international vocabulary.

citation.authors: Östen Dahl
citation.title: Tea (WALS Online chapter 138)

wals-139A.name: Irregular Negatives in Sign Languages
wals-139A.question: How many negation signs are irregular rather than regularly formed, in a sign language.

2.label: One
2.plain: One irregular negative

wals-139A.mt_relevance: Sign languages lack a standard written form, so this concerns sign-language (video) translation, not text MT.

citation.authors: Ulrike Zeshan
citation.title: Irregular Negatives in Sign Languages (WALS Online chapter 139)

wals-140A.name: Question Particles in Sign Languages
wals-140A.question: How many separate question particles (question-marking signs) a sign language has.

2.label: One
2.plain: One question particle

wals-140A.mt_relevance: Concerns manual question-marking signs; relevant to sign-language translation, not written text MT.

citation.authors: Ulrike Zeshan
citation.title: Question Particles in Sign Languages (WALS Online chapter 140)

wals-141A.name: Writing Systems
wals-141A.question: What kind of writing system the language uses (alphabet, syllabary, logographic, etc.).

2.label: Consonantal
2.plain: Consonantal

wals-141A.mt_relevance: Script type drives tokenization: logographic scripts run words together with no spaces, while consonantal scripts omit vowels — both strain MT tokenizers.

citation.authors: Bernard Comrie
citation.title: Writing Systems (WALS Online chapter 141)

wals-142A.name: Para-Linguistic Usages of Clicks

1.label: Logical meanings
1.plain: Clicks may express logical meanings ('yes' and/or 'no')

2.plain: Clicks may express affective but not logical meanings

3.label: Other or none
3.plain: Clicks may express neither affective nor logical meanings

wals-142A.mt_relevance: Paralinguistic clicks (like English 'tsk') are seldom written down, so this has little effect on text translation.

citation.authors: David Gil

wals-143A.property: Order of Negative Morpheme and Verb

2.label: VNeg

16.label: OptTripleNeg&ObligDoubleNeg

17.plain: Optional Triple Negation with Optional Double Negation

wals-143B.name: Obligatory Double Negation

16.plain: Obligatory double negation with optional triple negation

wals-143C.question: Whether a clause can optionally take a second negative word alongside the main negator.

23.plain: Optional double negation with optional triple negation

citation.authors: Matthew S. Dryer

citation.authors: Matthew S. Dryer

wals-143E.name: Preverbal Negative Morphemes
wals-143E.question: Whether negation is marked before the verb, as a separate word or a prefix.

2.label: [Neg-V]
2.plain: Negative prefix

3.label: NegV&[Neg-V]

citation.authors: Matthew S. Dryer
citation.title: Order of Negative Morpheme and Verb (WALS Online chapter 143)

wals-143F.name: Postverbal Negative Morphemes
wals-143F.question: Whether negation is marked after the verb, as a separate word or a suffix.

2.label: [V-Neg]
2.plain: Negative suffix

3.label: VNeg&[V-Neg]
3.plain: Both postverbal negative word and negative suffix

citation.authors: Matthew S. Dryer

wals-143G.property: Minor morphological means of signaling negation
wals-143G.name: Minor morphological means of signaling negation

2.label: NegInfix

citation.authors: Matthew S. Dryer

wals-144A.property: Position of Negative Word With Respect to Subject, Object, and Verb
