4.plain: Particle, a few lexical items may intervene

apics-46.mt_relevance: MT must know if the progressive marker is an affix or a movable particle to segment the verb and place intervening words right.

citation.authors: Michaelis, Susanne Maria, Philippe Maurer, Martin Haspelmath & Magnus Huber (eds.)
citation.title: Tightness of the link between the progressive marker and the verb (APiCS Online)

apics-47.name: Uses of the progressive marker
apics-47.question: Whether the ongoing-action ('-ing') marker also covers habits, states, or the future.

2.label: Only progressive function
2.plain: Only progressive function

8.label: Progressive, habitual, current state, and future
8.plain: Progressive, habitual, current state, and future

apics-47.mt_relevance: One progressive marker may map to several tenses; MT must decide whether it means ongoing, habitual, or future action.

citation.authors: Michaelis, Susanne Maria, Philippe Maurer, Martin Haspelmath & Magnus Huber (eds.)
citation.title: Uses of the progressive marker (APiCS Online)

apics-48.name: Uses of the habitual marker
apics-48.question: Whether the habitual ('usually does') marker also covers ongoing action or the future.

2.label: Only habitual function
2.plain: Only habitual function

9.label: Habitual, progressive, current state, and future
9.plain: Habitual, progressive, current state, and future

apics-48.mt_relevance: A single habitual marker can span habit, ongoing action, or future; MT must pick the reading the target tense system forces.

citation.authors: Michaelis, Susanne Maria, Philippe Maurer, Martin Haspelmath & Magnus Huber (eds.)
citation.title: Uses of the habitual marker (APiCS Online)

apics-49.name: Tense-aspect systems
apics-49.question: Whether verbs mark time (past/present), aspect (completed vs ongoing), or a mix of both.

2.label: Purely temporal system
2.plain: Purely temporal system

4.label: No or only one tense or aspect marker
4.plain: No or only one tense or aspect marker

apics-49.mt_relevance: When a language marks completed-vs-ongoing aspect instead of past/present tense, MT must invent the time cues the source never spelled out.

citation.authors: Michaelis, Susanne Maria, Philippe Maurer, Martin Haspelmath & Magnus Huber (eds.)
citation.title: Tense-aspect systems (APiCS Online)

apics-50.property: Negation and tense, aspect, and mood marking
apics-50.name: Negation and tense, aspect, and mood marking
apics-50.question: Whether negating a sentence changes, drops, or replaces its tense-aspect-mood markers.

1.label: Same TAM marking in negated clauses
1.plain: Same TAM marking in negated clauses

2.label: Reduced TAM marking in negated clauses
2.plain: Reduced TAM marking in negated clauses

3.label: Different TAM marking in negated clauses
3.plain: Different TAM marking in negated clauses

4.label: Reduced and different TAM marking in negated clauses
4.plain: Reduced and different TAM marking in negated clauses

apics-50.mt_relevance: If negation swaps or deletes tense-aspect markers, MT can't simply add 'not' and must reshape the verb, or it emits an ungrammatical negative.

citation.authors: Michaelis, Susanne Maria, Philippe Maurer, Martin Haspelmath & Magnus Huber (eds.)
citation.title: Negation and tense, aspect, and mood marking (APiCS Online)

apics-51.property: Present reference of stative verbs and past perfective reference of dynamic verbs
apics-51.name: Present reference of stative verbs and past perfective reference of dynamic verbs
apics-51.question: Whether an unmarked verb reads as present with state verbs but as past with action verbs.

1.label: Stative verbs with present reference and dynamic verbs with past perfective reference are both unmarked
1.plain: Stative verbs with present reference and dynamic verbs with past perfective reference are both unmarked

2.label: Stative verbs with present reference and dynamic verbs with past perfective reference are marked with the same overt marker
2.plain: Stative verbs with present reference and dynamic verbs with past perfective reference are marked with the same overt marker

3.label: Stative verbs with present reference and dynamic verbs with past perfective reference are marked differently
3.plain: Stative verbs with present reference and dynamic verbs with past perfective reference are marked differently

4.label: The language has no or only one TAM marker
4.plain: The language has no or only one TAM marker

apics-51.mt_relevance: A bare verb can mean 'knows' but also 'ran' depending on verb type, so MT must infer tense from whether the verb names a state or an action.

citation.authors: Michaelis, Susanne Maria, Philippe Maurer, Martin Haspelmath & Magnus Huber (eds.)
citation.title: Present reference of stative verbs and past perfective reference of dynamic verbs (APiCS Online)

apics-52.name: Aspect markers and inchoative meaning
apics-52.question: Whether an aspect marker on a state word like 'ripe' shifts it to 'becoming ripe'.

1.label: No inchoative meaning with aspect markers
1.plain: No inchoative meaning with aspect markers

2.label: Inchoative expressed by progressive marker
2.plain: Inchoative expressed by progressive marker

4.label: Inchoative expressed by progressive and completive markers
4.plain: Inchoative expressed by progressive and completive markers

apics-52.mt_relevance: 'Is ripening' versus 'is ripe' can hinge on one aspect marker, so MT may render a change-of-state the source only meant as ongoing or completed.

citation.authors: Michaelis, Susanne Maria, Philippe Maurer, Martin Haspelmath & Magnus Huber (eds.)
citation.title: Aspect markers and inchoative meaning (APiCS Online)

apics-53.name: Aspect change in verb chains
apics-53.question: Whether a second chained verb can take ongoing aspect while the first stays completed.

1.label: Aspect change in verb chains is possible
1.plain: Aspect change in verb chains is possible

2.label: Aspect change in verb chains is not possible
2.plain: Aspect change in verb chains is not possible

apics-53.mt_relevance: Chained verbs may background one action as ongoing against a completed one, a foreground/background contrast MT must keep or the event sequence blurs.

citation.authors: Michaelis, Susanne Maria, Philippe Maurer, Martin Haspelmath & Magnus Huber (eds.)
citation.title: Aspect change in verb chains (APiCS Online)

apics-54.property: Suppletion according to tense and aspect
apics-54.name: Suppletion according to tense and aspect
apics-54.question: Whether verbs use a different stem for different tenses or aspects, like 'go' vs 'went'.

1.label: Weak suppletion according to tense only
1.plain: Weak suppletion according to tense only

2.label: Strong suppletion according to tense only
2.plain: Strong suppletion according to tense only

3.label: Weak suppletion according to aspect only
3.plain: Weak suppletion according to aspect only

4.label: Strong suppletion according to aspect only
4.plain: Strong suppletion according to aspect only

5.label: Strong suppletion according to both tense and aspect
5.plain: Strong suppletion according to both tense and aspect

6.label: No suppletion according to tense or aspect
6.plain: No suppletion according to tense or aspect

apics-54.mt_relevance: Irregular stem swaps like go/went must be memorized, not derived, so rare or newly coined verbs are where MT most often emits a wrong or invented form.

citation.authors: Michaelis, Susanne Maria, Philippe Maurer, Martin Haspelmath & Magnus Huber (eds.)
citation.title: Suppletion according to tense and aspect (APiCS Online)

apics-55.name: Ability verb and epistemic possibility
apics-55.question: Whether one verb covers both 'can' (ability) and 'maybe' (possibility).

1.label: Ability verb also expresses epistemic possibility
1.plain: Ability verb also expresses epistemic possibility

2.label: Ability verb cannot express epistemic possibility
2.plain: Ability verb cannot express epistemic possibility

apics-55.mt_relevance: If 'can' also means 'maybe', MT must use context to choose between ability and likelihood, and choosing wrong flips what the sentence claims.

citation.authors: Michaelis, Susanne Maria, Philippe Maurer, Martin Haspelmath & Magnus Huber (eds.)
citation.title: Ability verb and epistemic possibility (APiCS Online)

apics-56.name: The prohibitive
apics-56.question: How the language forms a negative command like 'Don't go!'.

1.label: Normal imperative construction and normal negator
1.plain: Normal imperative construction and normal negator

2.label: Normal imperative construction and special negator
2.plain: Normal imperative construction and special negator

3.label: Special imperative construction and normal negator
3.plain: Special imperative construction and normal negator

4.label: Special imperative construction and special negator
4.plain: Special imperative construction and special negator

apics-56.mt_relevance: Negative commands may need a special 'don't' word or verb form unlike ordinary negation, so a literal 'not' plus command can come out ungrammatical.

citation.authors: Michaelis, Susanne Maria, Philippe Maurer, Martin Haspelmath & Magnus Huber (eds.)
citation.title: The prohibitive (APiCS Online)

apics-57.name: Marking of patient noun phrases
apics-57.question: Whether the object takes special marking, sometimes only when definite or animate.

2.label: Only definite patient NPs are marked
2.plain: Only definite patient NPs are marked

3.label: Only animate patient NPs are marked
3.plain: Only animate patient NPs are marked

4.label: Only definite and animate patient NPs are marked
4.plain: Only definite and animate patient NPs are marked

apics-57.mt_relevance: Object marking that shows up only for definite or animate nouns forces MT to track animacy and definiteness the source may leave implicit.

citation.authors: Michaelis, Susanne Maria, Philippe Maurer, Martin Haspelmath & Magnus Huber (eds.)
citation.title: Marking of patient noun phrases (APiCS Online)

apics-58.property: Alignment of case marking of full noun phrases
apics-58.name: Alignment of case marking of full noun phrases
apics-58.question: How the language marks who does an action versus who receives it (accusative vs ergative).

2.label: Accusative alignment
2.plain: Accusative alignment

apics-58.mt_relevance: Ergative systems mark a transitive subject unlike an intransitive one, so mapping onto a subject/object language can misassign who acted on whom.

citation.authors: Michaelis, Susanne Maria, Philippe Maurer, Martin Haspelmath & Magnus Huber (eds.)
citation.title: Alignment of case marking of full noun phrases (APiCS Online)

apics-59.property: Alignment of case marking of personal pronouns
apics-59.name: Alignment of case marking of personal pronouns
apics-59.question: Whether pronouns change form for subject vs object (like I/me), or stay the same.

2.label: Accusative alignment
2.plain: Accusative alignment

apics-59.mt_relevance: Pronoun case like 'I' vs 'me' must match each pronoun's role; a language that doesn't distinguish them gives MT no surface cue to the target form.

citation.authors: Michaelis, Susanne Maria, Philippe Maurer, Martin Haspelmath & Magnus Huber (eds.)
citation.title: Alignment of case marking of personal pronouns (APiCS Online)

apics-60.name: Ditransitive constructions with ‘give’
apics-60.question: How the language builds 'give' sentences with both a recipient and a thing given.

2.label: Indirect-object construction
2.plain: Indirect-object construction

apics-60.mt_relevance: Whether it's 'give John a book' or 'give a book to John' depends on this pattern, so MT must restructure the two objects, not map them word for word.

citation.authors: Michaelis, Susanne Maria, Philippe Maurer, Martin Haspelmath & Magnus Huber (eds.)
citation.title: Ditransitive constructions with ‘give’ (APiCS Online)

apics-61.property: Order of recipient and theme in ditransitive constructions
apics-61.name: Order of recipient and theme in ditransitive constructions
apics-61.question: Whether 'give'-type verbs put the recipient (who gets it) or the thing given first.

2.label: Subject – verb – theme – recipient
2.plain: Subject – verb – theme – recipient

apics-61.mt_relevance: Recipient/theme order signals who gets what, so getting it wrong makes MT confuse the person receiving with the thing given ('give John a book' vs 'give a book John').

citation.authors: Michaelis, Susanne Maria, Philippe Maurer, Martin Haspelmath & Magnus Huber (eds.)
citation.title: Order of recipient and theme in ditransitive constructions (APiCS Online)

apics-62.name: Expression of pronominal subjects
apics-62.question: How subjects like 'I' or 'she' appear — required words, affixes, or optional.

2.label: Pronoun affixes
2.plain: Pronoun affixes

apics-62.mt_relevance: Pro-drop languages omit subject pronouns, so MT must recover 'I' vs 'she' from context when the target language demands one.

citation.authors: Michaelis, Susanne Maria, Philippe Maurer, Martin Haspelmath & Magnus Huber (eds.)
citation.title: Expression of pronominal subjects (APiCS Online)

apics-63.name: Expletive subject in ‘seem’ constructions
apics-63.question: Whether 'seem' sentences use a dummy subject like the 'it' in 'it seems that…'.

2.label: An expletive subject is not used
2.plain: An expletive subject is not used

apics-63.mt_relevance: Languages without a dummy subject drop the 'it', so MT must insert or delete this meaningless placeholder when translating 'it seems'.

citation.authors: Michaelis, Susanne Maria, Philippe Maurer, Martin Haspelmath & Magnus Huber (eds.)
citation.title: Expletive subject in ‘seem’ constructions (APiCS Online)

apics-64.name: Expletive subject of existential verb
apics-64.question: Whether 'there is' clauses use a dummy subject like English 'there' or French 'il'.

2.label: An expletive subject is not used
2.plain: An expletive subject is not used

apics-64.mt_relevance: MT must add or drop the empty 'there'/'it' placeholder that existential clauses require in some languages but not others.

citation.authors: Michaelis, Susanne Maria, Philippe Maurer, Martin Haspelmath & Magnus Huber (eds.)
citation.title: Expletive subject of existential verb (APiCS Online)

apics-65.name: Raining constructions
apics-65.question: How the language says 'it is raining' — e.g. 'rain falls', 'it rains', or just 'rains'.

2.label: Rain rains
2.plain: Rain rains

apics-65.mt_relevance: Weather expressions rarely translate word-for-word, so MT must map 'it rains' onto forms like 'rain falls' that carry no dummy subject.

citation.authors: Michaelis, Susanne Maria, Philippe Maurer, Martin Haspelmath & Magnus Huber (eds.)
citation.title: Raining constructions (APiCS Online)

apics-66.name: Experiencer constructions with ‘headache’
apics-66.question: Whether a headache is framed as the person having it, the body-part, or the pain itself.

2.label: Body-part is subject
2.plain: Body-part is subject

apics-66.mt_relevance: MT must recast which noun is grammatical subject — 'she has a headache' vs 'the head hurts her' — a shift the source may not signal.

citation.authors: Michaelis, Susanne Maria, Philippe Maurer, Martin Haspelmath & Magnus Huber (eds.)
citation.title: Experiencer constructions with ‘headache’ (APiCS Online)

apics-67.name: Experiencer constructions with ‘like’
apics-67.question: Whether 'I like X' puts the liker as subject, object, or dative ('X pleases me').

2.label: Experiencer is object
2.plain: Experiencer is object

4.label: Both experiencer and stimulus are objects
4.plain: Both experiencer and stimulus are objects

apics-67.mt_relevance: MT must decide if the liker is subject ('I like it') or object ('it pleases me'), rearranging roles the source encodes differently.

citation.authors: Michaelis, Susanne Maria, Philippe Maurer, Martin Haspelmath & Magnus Huber (eds.)
citation.title: Experiencer constructions with ‘like’ (APiCS Online)

apics-68.name: Experiencer constructions with ‘fear’
apics-68.question: Whether 'being afraid' is a verb, an adjective, or has fear itself as the subject.

2.label: Experiencer is subject, 'fear' is non-verbal
2.plain: Experiencer is subject, 'fear' is non-verbal

apics-68.mt_relevance: MT must choose between verbal ('she fears') and non-verbal ('she is afraid') framings, and whether fear or the person is subject.

citation.authors: Michaelis, Susanne Maria, Philippe Maurer, Martin Haspelmath & Magnus Huber (eds.)
citation.title: Experiencer constructions with ‘fear’ (APiCS Online)

apics-69.name: Instrumental expressions
apics-69.question: How instruments like 'with a knife' are marked — preposition, verb, case, or nothing.

2.label: Serial verb
2.plain: Serial verb

apics-69.mt_relevance: Serial-verb languages express 'cut with a knife' as 'take knife cut', so MT cannot just map a preposition onto the instrument.

citation.authors: Michaelis, Susanne Maria, Philippe Maurer, Martin Haspelmath & Magnus Huber (eds.)
citation.title: Instrumental expressions (APiCS Online)

apics-70.name: Comitatives and instrumentals
apics-70.question: Whether 'with a friend' and 'with a knife' use the same word or different ones.

2.label: Differentiation
2.plain: Differentiation

apics-70.mt_relevance: If the source uses one 'with' for both company and tools, MT into a language that splits them must decide which meaning is intended.

citation.authors: Michaelis, Susanne Maria, Philippe Maurer, Martin Haspelmath & Magnus Huber (eds.)
citation.title: Comitatives and instrumentals (APiCS Online)

apics-71.name: Noun phrase conjunction and comitative
apics-71.question: Whether joining nouns ('John and Mary') uses the same word as 'with' ('John with Mary').

2.label: Differentiation
2.plain: Differentiation

apics-71.mt_relevance: When one word means both 'and' and 'with', MT must pick 'and' vs 'with' for the target language from context alone.

citation.authors: Michaelis, Susanne Maria, Philippe Maurer, Martin Haspelmath & Magnus Huber (eds.)
citation.title: Noun phrase conjunction and comitative (APiCS Online)

apics-72.name: Nominal and verbal conjunction
apics-72.question: Whether 'and' joining nouns is the same word as 'and' joining whole clauses.

2.label: Identity, expressed by juxtaposition
2.plain: Identity, expressed by juxtaposition

apics-72.mt_relevance: Some languages use different words for noun-'and' vs clause-'and', so MT must pick the right connective for what is being joined.

citation.authors: Michaelis, Susanne Maria, Philippe Maurer, Martin Haspelmath & Magnus Huber (eds.)
citation.title: Nominal and verbal conjunction (APiCS Online)

apics-73.name: Predicative noun phrases
apics-73.question: Whether 'Mary is a singer' needs a linking verb ('is') or joins the words directly.

2.label: No copula
2.plain: No copula

apics-73.mt_relevance: Copula-less languages say 'Mary singer', so MT must insert or delete the linking 'is' when translating class-membership clauses.

citation.authors: Michaelis, Susanne Maria, Philippe Maurer, Martin Haspelmath & Magnus Huber (eds.)
citation.title: Predicative noun phrases (APiCS Online)

apics-74.name: Predicative adjectives
apics-74.question: Whether 'Mary is old' needs a linking verb (copula) or just joins adjective to subject.

2.label: No copula
2.plain: No copula

apics-74.mt_relevance: In no-copula creoles adjectives act like verbs, so translating into English forces inserting an 'is/are' the source never wrote.

citation.authors: Michaelis, Susanne Maria, Philippe Maurer, Martin Haspelmath & Magnus Huber (eds.)
citation.title: Predicative adjectives (APiCS Online)

apics-75.name: Predicative locative phrases
apics-75.question: Whether 'Mary is in town' uses a linking verb (copula) or none.

2.label: No copula
2.plain: No copula

apics-75.mt_relevance: Some creoles drop the copula before a place phrase, so MT into a copula language must supply the missing 'is/are'.

citation.authors: Michaelis, Susanne Maria, Philippe Maurer, Martin Haspelmath & Magnus Huber (eds.)
citation.title: Predicative locative phrases (APiCS Online)

apics-76.property: Predicative noun phrases and predicative locative phrases
apics-76.name: Predicative noun phrases and predicative locative phrases
apics-76.question: Whether 'I am a teacher' and 'I am in town' use the same construction or different ones.

2.label: Differentiation
2.plain: Differentiation

apics-76.mt_relevance: If one predicate takes a copula and the other doesn't, MT must choose the right pattern per clause instead of applying one blanket rule.

citation.authors: Michaelis, Susanne Maria, Philippe Maurer, Martin Haspelmath & Magnus Huber (eds.)
citation.title: Predicative noun phrases and predicative locative phrases (APiCS Online)

apics-77.name: Predicative possession
apics-77.question: How the language says someone 'has' something (e.g. 'John has a horse').

2.label: Comitative
2.plain: Comitative

apics-77.mt_relevance: Possession may be built with 'have', 'with', or 'to-me-is', so MT must remap the whole clause rather than swap in one verb.

citation.authors: Michaelis, Susanne Maria, Philippe Maurer, Martin Haspelmath & Magnus Huber (eds.)
citation.title: Predicative possession (APiCS Online)

apics-78.property: Existential verb and transitive possession verb
apics-78.name: Existential verb and transitive possession verb
apics-78.question: Whether the word for 'there is' is the same as the word for 'have'.

2.label: Differentiation
2.plain: Differentiation

apics-78.mt_relevance: When one verb covers both 'there is' and 'have', MT must decide from context which English verb the same source word should become.

citation.authors: Michaelis, Susanne Maria, Philippe Maurer, Martin Haspelmath & Magnus Huber (eds.)
citation.title: Existential verb and transitive possession verb (APiCS Online)

apics-79.name: Going to named places
apics-79.question: How the language marks going to a named place (e.g. 'to Leipzig').

2.label: Preposition
2.plain: Preposition

apics-79.mt_relevance: Direction 'to a place' may be shown by a preposition, a case ending, or a serial verb, so MT can't just map it onto English 'to'.

citation.authors: Michaelis, Susanne Maria, Philippe Maurer, Martin Haspelmath & Magnus Huber (eds.)
citation.title: Going to named places (APiCS Online)

apics-80.name: Coming from named places
apics-80.question: How the language marks coming from a named place (e.g. 'from Belair').

2.label: Preposition
2.plain: Preposition

apics-80.mt_relevance: Source 'from a place' may be marked by a preposition, a case ending, or a serial verb, so MT can't assume one 'from' word maps across.

citation.authors: Michaelis, Susanne Maria, Philippe Maurer, Martin Haspelmath & Magnus Huber (eds.)
citation.title: Coming from named places (APiCS Online)

apics-81.name: Motion-to and motion-from
apics-81.question: Whether going to and coming from a place use the same marker or different ones.

2.label: Differentiation
2.plain: Differentiation

apics-81.mt_relevance: European lexifiers split to/from, but a creole may use one marker for both, so MT must add the direction English keeps separate.

citation.authors: Michaelis, Susanne Maria, Philippe Maurer, Martin Haspelmath & Magnus Huber (eds.)
citation.title: Motion-to and motion-from (APiCS Online)

apics-82.name: Transitive motion verbs: ‘push’
apics-82.question: How the language marks pushing something to a place (motion toward a goal).

2.label: At-rest marking is used to express motion-to
2.plain: At-rest marking is used to express motion-to

apics-82.mt_relevance: 'Push X into Y' may reuse a static 'at' marker or a serial verb, so MT must infer the motion English shows with 'into' or 'to'.

citation.authors: Michaelis, Susanne Maria, Philippe Maurer, Martin Haspelmath & Magnus Huber (eds.)
citation.title: Transitive motion verbs: ‘push’ (APiCS Online)

apics-83.name: Transitive motion verbs: ‘pull’
apics-83.question: How the language marks pulling something from a place (motion away from a source).

2.label: At-rest marking is used to express motion-from
2.plain: At-rest marking is used to express motion-from

apics-83.mt_relevance: 'Pull X out of Y' may reuse a static 'in' marker, so MT must recover the 'out of' direction the source clause leaves implicit.

citation.authors: Michaelis, Susanne Maria, Philippe Maurer, Martin Haspelmath & Magnus Huber (eds.)
citation.title: Transitive motion verbs: ‘pull’ (APiCS Online)

apics-84.property: Directional serial verb constructions with 'come' and 'go'
apics-84.name: Directional serial verb constructions with 'come' and 'go'
apics-84.question: Whether the language uses 'come'/'go' as a second verb to show an action's direction.

2.label: ‘Come’ and ‘go’ directionals do not exist
2.plain: ‘Come’ and ‘go’ directionals do not exist

apics-84.mt_relevance: Direction carried by a serial 'come/go' has no one-word English match, so MT must fold it into a preposition or a verb like 'bring/take'.

citation.authors: Michaelis, Susanne Maria, Philippe Maurer, Martin Haspelmath & Magnus Huber (eds.)
citation.title: Directional serial verb constructions with 'come' and 'go' (APiCS Online)

apics-85.name: ‘Take’ serial verb constructions
apics-85.question: Whether the language uses a serial verb 'take' to introduce an instrument or object.

1.label: Theme of the second verb, literal interpretation possible
1.plain: Theme of the second verb, literal interpretation possible

2.label: Theme of the second verb, literal interpretation impossible
2.plain: Theme of the second verb, literal interpretation impossible

3.label: Instrument of the second verb, no resumptive pronoun
3.plain: Instrument of the second verb, no resumptive pronoun

4.label: Instrument of the second verb, with resumptive pronoun
4.plain: Instrument of the second verb, with resumptive pronoun

apics-85.mt_relevance: A serial 'take' marks the tool or object other languages show with 'with' or case, so MT must reinterpret it, not translate 'take' literally.

citation.authors: Michaelis, Susanne Maria, Philippe Maurer, Martin Haspelmath & Magnus Huber (eds.)
citation.title: ‘Take’ serial verb constructions (APiCS Online)

apics-86.name: 'Give' serial verb constructions
apics-86.question: Whether the language uses a serial verb 'give' to mark a recipient or beneficiary.

2.label: ‘Give’ in second position, recipient or beneficiary
2.plain: ‘Give’ in second position, recipient or beneficiary

apics-86.mt_relevance: A serial 'give' marks who benefits, matching English 'to/for', so MT must render it as a preposition rather than a second 'give' verb.

citation.authors: Michaelis, Susanne Maria, Philippe Maurer, Martin Haspelmath & Magnus Huber (eds.)
citation.title: 'Give' serial verb constructions (APiCS Online)

apics-87.name: Reflexive constructions
apics-87.question: How the language says a subject acts on itself, as in 'he hurt himself'.

2.label: Implicit expression
2.plain: Implicit expression

apics-87.mt_relevance: Reflexive strategies vary (self-pronoun, verb marking, 'body' word); MT must map the source's method onto the target's, adding words like 'himself' where none appear.

citation.authors: Michaelis, Susanne Maria, Philippe Maurer, Martin Haspelmath & Magnus Huber (eds.)
citation.title: Reflexive constructions (APiCS Online)

apics-88.name: Intensifiers and reflexive pronouns
apics-88.question: Whether the emphatic 'himself' and the reflexive 'himself' are the same word.

2.label: Intensifiers and reflexives are differentiated
2.plain: Intensifiers and reflexives are differentiated

apics-88.mt_relevance: When one form covers both emphasis and reflexivity, MT can misread which is meant, e.g. rendering 'the king himself came' as if the king acted on himself.

citation.authors: Michaelis, Susanne Maria, Philippe Maurer, Martin Haspelmath & Magnus Huber (eds.)
citation.title: Intensifiers and reflexive pronouns (APiCS Online)

apics-89.name: Reciprocal constructions
apics-89.question: How the language expresses 'each other,' and whether it reuses the reflexive form.

2.label: Identical and special reciprocal construction
2.plain: Identical and special reciprocal construction

apics-89.mt_relevance: If reciprocal and reflexive share a form, MT may confuse 'they saw themselves' with 'they saw each other,' flipping who did what to whom.

citation.authors: Michaelis, Susanne Maria, Philippe Maurer, Martin Haspelmath & Magnus Huber (eds.)
citation.title: Reciprocal constructions (APiCS Online)

apics-90.name: Passive constructions
apics-90.question: Whether and how the language forms passives like 'the door was opened'.

2.label: Passive without verbal coding
2.plain: Passive without verbal coding

apics-90.mt_relevance: Passives here may lack verb marking or use odd auxiliaries, so MT must spot a passive with no 'was …-ed' cue and place the agent right.

citation.authors: Michaelis, Susanne Maria, Philippe Maurer, Martin Haspelmath & Magnus Huber (eds.)
